{{Short description|German physicist and cosmologist}}
'''Raphael Flauger''' is a German theoretical physicist and cosmologist.<ref name=vita>{{cite web|author=Flauger, Raphael Manfred|title=Constraining Fundamental Physics with Cosmology|publisher=University of Texas at Austin|date=August 2009|url=https://repositories.lib.utexas.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/c0e490b5-98ef-4d8c-af5b-79e179e53eab/content}} (Doctoral Dissertation with Vita on p. 321)</ref>

==Education and career==
After receiving in June 1998 the ''[[Abitur]]'' from the Leibniz-Gymnasium in [[Altdorf bei Nürnberg]], Raphael Flauger entered in July 1998 the German Air Force for his compulsory military service. In October 1998 he enrolled in a long-distance education program in mechanical engineering offered by [[TU Dresden]]. After the completion of his military service in April 1999, he enrolled in the physics program at the [[University of Würzburg]]. There he received the ''[[Vordiplom]]'' in August 2000. He continued to study physics at the University of Würzburg until July 2001. In 2001 he joined the Weinberg Theory Group at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] (UT Austin). There in August 2002, he receive an M.A. in physics under the supervision of Sonia Paban. In autumn 2002, Flauger matriculated at [[Imperial College London]]. There in September 2003, he received an M.S in Quantum Fields and Fundamental Forces under the supervision of [[Arkady Tseytlin]]. After received his M.S., Flauger returned, as a Ph.D. student, to study with the Weinberg Theory Group at UT Austin. From January to August, he was a Graduate Fellow at the [[Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics]] (KITP). In August 2009 at UT Austin, he successfully defended his doctoral dissertation entitled ''Constraining Fundamental Physics with Cosmology''. His doctor supervisor was [[Steven Weinberg]]. In addition to Weinberg, Flauger's doctoral committee consisted of Arno Bohm, [[Willy Fischler]], [[Dan Freed]], and Sonia Paban.<ref name=vita/>

As a postdoc, Flauger did research from 2009 to 2011 at [[Yale University]]. From 2011 to 2014 he was a postdoctoral fellow at [[New York University]], as well as a temporary member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref name=IAS/> He was from 2014 to 2015 an assistant professor at [[Carnegie Mellon University]]<ref name=Sloan>{{cite web|url=https://www.cmu.edu/physics/news-events/news-archive/2015/flauger-sloan.html|title=''Prof. Raphael Flauger Wins Sloan Research Fellowship''|website=Department of Physics, Carnegie Mellon University|date=February 25, 2015}}</ref> and from 2015<ref name=NewHorizons>{{cite web|title=Raphael Flauger, 2016 New Horizons in Physics Prize|website=breakthroughprize.org|url=https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/1/L159}}</ref> to 2019 an assistant professor at UT Austin. In 2019 he joined, as an associate professor, the physics department of the [[University of California, San Diego]],<ref name=IAS>{{cite web|title=Raphael Flauger|website=Institute for Advanced Study|date=9 December 2019 |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/raphael-flauger}}</ref> where he is now a full professor.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://physics.ucsd.edu/people/profile?id=rmflauger | title=Profile: Raphael Flauger &#124; Department of Physics |website=University of California, San Diego}}</ref>

Flauger is interested in predictions about the early universe from the [[Cosmic background radiation|Cosmic Microwave Background]] (CMB), in particular from the data of the [[Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe]] (WMAP) and the [[Planck (spacecraft)|Planck space-based observatory]]. He is also interested in [[quantum field theories]], [[quantum gravity]] and [[string theory]] (both with [[Phenomenological quantum gravity|phenomenological model]]s and with formal aspects).

In 2014, Flauger played a key role in criticizing and refuting the then sensational claims of the [[BICEP and Keck Array#BICEP2|BICEP2]] collaboration (2nd generation of Background Imaging of Cosmic Extragalactic Polarization project) to have found [[gravitational waves]] and evidence of [[inflation (cosmology)|inflation]] in the CMB (even before the analysis of the Planck telescope team). At that time (2013–2014) he was at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/ideas/2014/flauger-bicep |title=BICEP: Spacetime Ripples or Galaxy Dust? - Ideas &#124; Institute for Advanced Study |date=23 September 2014 }}</ref><ref name=IAS/> He was the lead author of an article, published in May 2014, indicating that polarized emission from interstellar dust could explain the findings of the BICEP2 science team.<ref>{{cite news|author=Achenbach, Joel|author-link=Joel Achenbach|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=May 16, 2014|title=Big Bang backlash: BICEP2 discovery of gravity waves questioned by cosmologists|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/big-bang-backlash-bicep2-discovery-of-gravity-waves-questioned-by-cosmologists/2014/05/16/e575b2fc-db07-11e3-bda1-9b46b2066796_story.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Achenbach, Joel|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=May 29, 2014|title=Big Bang rumblings: What it all means|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/achenblog/wp/2014/05/29/is-that-the-fingerprint-of-the-big-bang-or-just-foreground-dust/}}</ref>

As a doctoral student of Weinberg at UT Austin, Flauger had predicted the B-modes in the CMB as an indication of gravitational waves that the BICEP2 science team thought they had found.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.75.123505 |title=Tensor microwave background fluctuations for large multipole order |date=2007 |last1=Flauger |first1=Raphael |last2=Weinberg |first2=Steven |journal=Physical Review D |volume=75 |issue=12 |article-number=123505 |arxiv=astro-ph/0703179 |bibcode=2007PhRvD..75l3505F }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=astro-ph/0703179 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.75.123505 | title=Tensor microwave background fluctuations for large multipole order | date=2007 | last1=Flauger | first1=Raphael | last2=Weinberg | first2=Steven | journal=Physical Review D | volume=75 | issue=12 | article-number=123505 | bibcode=2007PhRvD..75l3505F }}</ref> Flauger then worked on phenomenological string theory models that predict observably large B-modes, whereas previously it was generally assumed that such B-modes would not be predicted in string theory models because the associated energies are close to the [[Grand Unified Theory|GUT]] scale. According to Flauger and colleagues, this also opened up the possibility of testing string theory with CMB data. For example, he searched with [[Eva Silverstein]] and Liam McAllister for [[axion]] signals in the CMB, which are predicted by some string theories.

In 2015 Flauger received a two-year [[Sloan Research Fellowship]].<ref name=Sloan/> In 2016 he was awarded a [[New Horizons in Physics Prize]].<ref name=NewHorizons/>
